To different degrees, residents’ views on street lighting were mixed within each area, and this often reflects very localized aspects of lighting (for example, good or bad lighting directly outside the respondent’s house, in their back lane, or in a feature they use frequently such as a subway). Further, though lighting may appear to be adequate from the coverage map, in many areas it is not always working. These micro features of lighting are often what determines satisfaction, yet they are difficult to convey accurately on coverage maps. This is only one aspect of street lighting that would influence residents’ satisfaction with it. Poor street lighting can create a range of other problems with getting around (Herbert and Davidson, 1995; Painter, 1992; 1996; Townshend, 1997), especially for residents with a disability or those 21 who had young children. Being partially sighted, residents showed concerns of falling when walking in the dark (Pain, 2006). In the same survey, only a minority of residents felt that crime was also made worse by poor street lighting, such as burglary or vandalism. However, most of those questioned did not believe that street lighting had a significant impact on crime levels. Many expressed a belief that crime had deeper causes and would happen anyway, even in daylight. Some proposed that, in some instances, lighting actually helps criminals such as identifying victims or making it easier for them to see what they are doing. There was also strong feeling, in particular, that improved lighting would not help with the problems many residents perceived were to do with youth disorder. Here, it was felt that the relationship was more likely to be inverse. Many also said that children in their areas vandalized streetlights before committing petty crimes such as graffiti, so again the relationship is not straightforward (Pain, 2006). Residents’ perceptions of the relationships between street lighting and the incidence of crime, then, are reflexive and critical. Research surveys have tended to be premised and designed on the basis of fairly simple cause-and-effect relationships, but such relationships were dismissed by the majority of those interviewed; at most, street lighting was held to have a marginal and even then contradictory influence on local rates of crime. 2.2.2.2.2 Street Lighting and Fear of Crime Compared to resident’s views of the relationship between street lighting and crime, generally different views were observed in terms of fear of crime. Fear of crime, or perceived personal safety, is defined as a person’s immediate sense of security, and an absence of anxiety of becoming victimized, when traveling through a particular environment (Blöbaum, 2005). Street lighting is generally seen as the most important physical feature of an environment to affect the fear (Loewen, 1993; Nasar, 1993; Nasar, 1997). The amount and uniformity of illuminance, and perhaps also light spectrum, are found to affect perceived personal safety (Boyce, 2000; Knight, 2009).
